tagline: An Olmsted parkway follows the hills above the Providence River
intro: Veterans Memorial Parkway bends and changes elevation with the rolling ground above the Providence River. The 2.4-mile East Providence drive runs from Second Street to Route 103, lined with mature maple, oak, black pine and sycamore. RIDOT identifies its river and downtown skyline views, wooded setting and Olmsted design as defining features of the scenic roadway, designated in November 1991. RIDOT describes an entirely urban route whose adjoining woods screen parts of the city, allowing a changing sequence of neighborhood, river and skyline views.

Built between 1910 and 1920, the parkway belonged to the Greater Metropolitan Park Plan for Providence. The Olmsted firm designed it. Decades later, East Bay Bike Path construction and proposed changes to guardrails and mature trees brought its landscape under scrutiny. Concern over those changes led to the 1991 scenic-road nomination.

Heading south from Second Street near the Washington Bridge, the road rounds Fort Hill and follows the river escarpment toward Lyon Avenue. The East Bay Bike Path parallels its western side. The road then turns away from the river and descends to the causeway and bridge across Watchemoket Cove. Beyond the cove it rises again, passing Squantum Woods on the way to Pawtucket Avenue.

moments.title: Fort Hill Overlook
moments.text: Fort Hill puts the parkway above the Providence River, with views toward the city and port. Across from the overlook is the site of a fort built in 1775 to protect the harbor from the British. The overlook itself belongs to a later landscape plan. The 1999 stewardship plan records that the original Olmsted design was never fully implemented. It also describes trees and shrubs closing off views of the river, port and city, and proposes clearing and ongoing vegetation management. The bike path runs along the parkway’s west side beside the hilltop overlook.

moments.title: Watchemoket Cove
moments.text: At Watchemoket Cove, the parkway drops from the river heights to a causeway and bridge before climbing again. The cove is a tidal pond that the 1999 stewardship plan identifies as valuable habitat for migratory birds. The East Bay Bike Path follows a different crossing, using the railroad right-of-way across the cove. The plan proposed improving an informal parking area by the pumping station into a scenic stop. The changing elevation was part of the road’s design: the middle section approaches water level, while the southern portion winds through glacial outwash hills.

moments.title: Squantum Point
moments.text: Squantum Point’s clubhouse is the third in a succession of gathering places. Providence merchants and sea captains once traveled to an island south of the point for clambakes. After the island’s owner objected, Shubael Cady bought the point. The first clubhouse, an open-framed pavilion, followed in 1871. The present Colonial Revival clubhouse dates to 1900 and overlooks the Providence River from a rocky promontory. The Squantum Association is a private club; its clubhouse entered the National Register in 1980. The association later bought the island in 1912, linked it by a causeway in 1914 and built a pagoda there in 1916.
